difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: direct recall of three standard data-structure facts (a queue is FIFO, a stack is LIFO, a hash table supports fast lookup) in a single matching step; well under a minute for a prepared student.
stem:
Match the items in **Column 1** with the items in **Column 2** in the following table:

| Column 1 | Column 2 |
|---|---|
| (p) First In First Out | (i) Stacks |
| (q) Lookup Operation | (ii) Queues |
| (r) Last In First Out | (iii) Hash Tables |

solution.quick: First In First Out is the access rule of a **queue** (ii). Last In First Out is the access rule of a **stack** (i). A **hash table** exists to support fast lookup by key, in expected $O(1)$ time (iii). So the matching is (p) − (ii), (q) − (iii), (r) − (i) → **(A)**.

steps.title: (p) First In First Out → Queues (ii)
steps.body:
A **queue** inserts at the rear (*enqueue*) and removes from the front (*dequeue*). The element that has waited longest always leaves first.

Example: enqueue $1, 2, 3$; the first dequeue returns $1$, the element that went in first. This is **FIFO**, so (p) → (ii).

steps.title: (r) Last In First Out → Stacks (i)
steps.body:
A **stack** inserts (*push*) and removes (*pop*) at the same end, the top. The most recently inserted element always leaves first.

Example: push $1, 2, 3$; the first pop returns $3$, the element that went in last. This is **LIFO**, so (r) → (i).

steps.title: (q) Lookup Operation → Hash Tables (iii)
steps.body:
A **hash table** stores key–value pairs. A hash function $h(k)$ maps each key directly to a bucket index, so **lookup** (search by key), insertion and deletion take **expected $O(1)$** time. The worst case, when many keys collide, is $O(n)$.

Stacks and queues expose only one end, so finding an arbitrary element in them needs an $O(n)$ scan. Lookup is the operation hash tables are designed for, so (q) → (iii).

steps.title: Select the option
steps.body:
The complete matching is

$$
\text{(p)} - \text{(ii)}, \quad \text{(q)} - \text{(iii)}, \quad \text{(r)} - \text{(i)},
$$

which is exactly option **(A)**.

Check by elimination: only (A) and (B) pair (p) with (ii). Of these, (B) pairs lookup with stacks, which is wrong, so (A) remains.

solution.teaching:
**Abstract data types are defined by their operations.** A data structure is characterised by which element it hands back to you and how quickly it does so.

**Stack (LIFO: Last In, First Out).** Think of a pile of plates: you add to the top and take from the top.

- Operations: `push(x)` and `pop()`, both $O(1)$, plus `peek()` to read the top.
- Uses: the function-call stack (recursion), undo in editors, matching parentheses, evaluating postfix expressions, iterative DFS.
- In Python, a `list` with `append()` and `pop()`.

**Queue (FIFO: First In, First Out).** Think of a line at a ticket counter: people join at the back and are served from the front.

- Operations: `enqueue(x)` at the rear and `dequeue()` from the front, both $O(1)$ with a circular array or a linked list.
- Uses: BFS, CPU and printer scheduling, buffering data streams.
- In Python, `collections.deque` with `append()` and `popleft()`.

**Hash table (fast lookup).** It stores key–value pairs in an array of buckets. A hash function turns a key into an index, so you jump straight to the right bucket instead of scanning.

- Two keys that land in the same bucket cause a *collision*, which is handled by chaining (a list per bucket) or open addressing (probing for another slot).
- With a good hash function and a bounded load factor, search, insert and delete take **expected $O(1)$** time.
- Python's `dict` and `set` are hash tables.

**Back to this question.** FIFO names the queue discipline, LIFO names the stack discipline, and "lookup" is the operation hash tables are built for. That gives (p) − (ii), (q) − (iii), (r) − (i), which is option (A).

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: FIFO → queues, lookup → hash tables, LIFO → stacks. All three pairs are right.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: (p) − (ii) is right, but this option pairs lookup with stacks and LIFO with hash tables. A stack exposes only its top element, and a hash table has no insertion-order discipline.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: All three pairs are wrong. Stacks are LIFO, not FIFO. Queues are not a lookup structure. Hash tables do not follow LIFO order.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: (q) − (iii) is right, but stacks and queues are swapped. FIFO belongs to queues, and LIFO belongs to stacks.

solution.shortcut: Fix the most familiar pair first: FIFO = queue, so only (A) and (B) survive. Then lookup = hash table picks (A).
solution.commonTrap: Swapping stack and queue, which gives option (D): it gets the hash-table pair right but reverses FIFO and LIFO. A stack of plates is Last In, First Out; a queue at a counter is First In, First Out.

answerVerification.checkCode:
from collections import deque
q = deque()
for i in (1, 2, 3): q.append(i)          # enqueue 1, 2, 3
print("queue removes:", q.popleft())      # 1 -> First In First Out
s = []
for i in (1, 2, 3): s.append(i)          # push 1, 2, 3
print("stack removes:", s.pop())          # 3 -> Last In First Out
h = {"apple": 5, "kiwi": 7}               # Python dict = hash table
print("lookup kiwi:", h["kiwi"])          # direct lookup by key, expected O(1)
match = {"p": "ii", "q": "iii", "r": "i"} # FIFO-Queues, Lookup-Hash Tables, LIFO-Stacks
opts = {"A": {"p": "ii", "q": "iii", "r": "i"}, "B": {"p": "ii", "q": "i", "r": "iii"},
        "C": {"p": "i", "q": "ii", "r": "iii"}, "D": {"p": "i", "q": "iii", "r": "ii"}}
print("matching option:", [k for k, v in opts.items() if v == match])   # ['A']
